Consult Summary:
- 53-year-old male with one week of non-painful swelling and local warmth over the left elbow; clinical impression of left olecranon bursitis; plan includes NSAIDs, blood tests, and follow-up.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Swelling of the left elbow noticed about one week ago, described as non-painful, slightly warm, and possibly containing fluid.
- Associated symptoms: No pain, no significant functional limitation, no trauma or injury; able to move elbow normally.
- Pertinent negatives: No prior episodes of similar swelling; no family history of rheumatologic diseases reported; no widespread dry skin or eczema.
- Past medical history: Osteoarthritis diagnosed by a GP a few years ago.
- Allergies: Peanuts.
- Medication allergies: None known.
- Regular medications: None.
- Social history: Works a desk job (not physically demanding); participates in running 2–3 times weekly; otherwise healthy and active.
- Preventive care: Not mentioned.

Examination:
- Visual assessment via video: Swelling over the tip of the left elbow, appears slightly warm to touch (compared to surrounding skin), mild local tenderness adjacent to the swelling, skin noted as a bit dry over the tip, no significant erythema described.
- Vitals: Not documented.

Impression:
- Likely left olecranon bursitis (non-septic).

Plan:
- Start ibuprofen 400 mg twice daily after food (advised to stop if heartburn occurs).
- Arrange blood tests: inflammatory markers, infection screen, rheumatological antibodies, and gout screen.
- Blood test order forms to be mailed to patient with instructions; patient to have blood tests done at their convenience.
- Results expected in 5–6 days after blood draw.
- Follow-up (virtual or face-to-face) after blood test results to review ongoing symptoms and test results.
- Safety net advice: Seek urgent assessment if elbow becomes very red, painful, or if redness spreads/worsens (to rule out septic arthritis).
- Reassured patient that condition does not currently appear dangerous or life-threatening.

Quality checks:

●	Missing but clinically expected elements: No documentation of full review of systems, immunization status, or detailed functional impact; medication reconciliation limited to patient self-report; no explicit documentation of full physical exam or vitals.
●	Internal conflicts: None identified.
●	Transcript quality: Clear and detailed; minor conversational fillers and slight repetition noted but no loss of clinical information.
